Brendan Coffey, The Motley Fool

Investing in the final frontier offers massive potential for growth but requires careful navigation of complex technology. Here is how AST SpaceMobile (NASDAQ:ASTS) and Firefly Aerospace (NASDAQ:FLY) compare today.

AST SpaceMobile is building a global cellular network to connect smartphones directly via satellite, while Firefly Aerospace provides launch and orbital services for government and commercial missions. Both companies are scaling rapidly in a high-stakes environment, making them key candidates for investors looking to gain exposure to the modern space economy.

The case for AST SpaceMobile

AST SpaceMobile is building a space-based cellular broadband network designed to connect directly with standard smartphones without the need for special hardware. The company aims to disrupt the communication stocks landscape by providing seamless global coverage through revenue-sharing models with existing providers. It maintains partnerships with more than 50 mobile network operators, including AT&T Corp. (NYSE:T), Verizon Communications (NYSE:VZ), and Vodafone (NASDAQ:VOD).

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $71 million, representing a significant increase of approximately 1,500% over the previous year. Despite this growth, the company reported a net loss of close to $342 million for the same period. This resulted in a net margin of negative 482%.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 1.2x, which represents total debt relative to shareholder equity. The so-called current ratio, which measures the ability to cover short-term liabilities with short-term assets, is approximately 16.4x. Free cash flow for the period was roughly negative $1.1 billion, which is calculated as cash from operations minus capital expenditures.

The case for Firefly Aerospace

Firefly Aerospace serves as an end-to-end space and defense technology company that helps customers launch, land, and operate in orbit. Its customer base includes high-profile organizations such as NASA, the U.S. Space Force, Lockheed Martin Corp. (NYSE:LMT), and Northrop Grumman Corp. (NYSE:NOC). The company currently reports a backlog of approximately $1.4 billion, supported by multi-launch agreements and milestone-based billing.

In FY 2025, revenue for Firefly Aerospace reached nearly $160 million, a growth of approximately 160% compared to the prior year. The company reported a net loss of about $298.3 million for the period. This indicates a net margin of negative 187%.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.3x, which compares total debt to shareholder equity. Its current ratio stands at roughly 4.5x, indicating the company's liquidity position relative to its upcoming obligations. Free cash flow for the fiscal period was nearly negative $238 million, representing cash from operations minus capital expenditures.

On October 8, 2026, an ARK Invest fund sold 29,048 shares of SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX). At that day's close, the shares were worth about $4.7 million. The stock fell 4.19% that session and closed at $160.57.

Marco Bello/Getty Images

At 4:17 p.m. ET, after the close, Grain Management announced a definitive agreement to sell its nationwide 800 MHz spectrum portfolio to SpaceX. ARK's funds trade during market hours, so the sale went through before anyone outside the deal knew about it. That timing was unlucky, and the wireless carriers turned out to be the bigger story.

On October 9, T-Mobile (NASDAQ:TMUS) fell 13.27%, AT&T (NYSE:T) fell 9.81%, and Verizon (NYSE:VZ) fell 8.75%. SpaceX rose a more modest 1.25% to $162.57.

How the Sale and the Announcement Lined Up
SPCX Analyst Ratings — 24/7 Wall St.

ARK releases each day's trades after the market closes, so the October 8 trim only became public after Grain's news was already out. That disclosure order is why the trade looks well timed in hindsight.

ARK also sold 54,873 shares on October 6, worth about $9.4 million. It reportedly sold another 22,276 shares on October 9, after the news was public. If ARK had known about the deal, selling into it would make little sense.

title: AT&T (T) Got Hit by a SpaceX Scare. Is Its Moat Really Cracking?
detail:
AT&T (T) Got Hit by a SpaceX Scare. Is Its Moat Really Cracking?
Maham Fatima
Mon, October 12, 2026 at 5:39 AM PDT 5 min read
T
SPCX
VZ
TMUS
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

One headline from SpaceX was enough to rattle the biggest names in US telecom. According to CNBC, SpaceX struck a deal to acquire a spectrum license this week, and shares of AT&T (NYSE:T), Verizon, and T-Mobile all took a beating as investors pictured satellites beaming service straight to phones.

AT&T makes money two ways most people touch daily: wireless plans on smartphones and high-speed internet piped into homes and businesses, mostly over fiber. Both come as monthly subscriptions, which makes for a steady stream of cash, a predictability that regularly places entry-level telecom plays on lists like the 10 Best Stocks for Beginners with Little Money.

So is the sell-off a sign the moat is cracking, or a scare that misreads where AT&T's real edge sits? The answer depends less on what's happening in orbit than on what's buried under neighborhood streets.

AT&T (T) Got Hit by a SpaceX Scare. Is Its Moat Really Cracking?
Fiber Is the Real Fortress

AT&T's advantage isn't just its wireless network. It's the pairing of wireless with fiber, and that pairing is getting tighter. In the second quarter of 2026, 42.5% of households with AT&T's advanced home internet also took its wireless service. Customers who bundle tend to stick around, since leaving means rewiring both the phone bill and the home connection.

The numbers back it up. Postpaid phone churn (the share of monthly subscribers who leave) came in at just 0.86% in the second quarter, while the company added 432,000 postpaid phone customers. It also added 367,000 fiber subscribers and 279,000 fixed wireless customers in the same stretch.

The footprint keeps growing, too. AT&T reached 38.6 million fiber locations, adding more than 1 million during the quarter, and aims for more than 40 million by the end of 2026 and more than 60 million by 2030. The Lumen fiber deal, which closed earlier this year, feeds that push, a strategy that also sets it apart from cable-reliant broadband rivals.

The Shrinking Past Barely Matters

The growth side now carries the company. Advanced Connectivity service revenue reached $23.5 billion in the second quarter, up 5.1%, while the legacy business saw revenue drop 25.9%. Management expects that legacy unit to become immaterial by the end of 2029.

That shift shows up in profits. Adjusted EPS rose to $0.65 from $0.54 a year earlier, and free cash flow hit $4.7 billion. Management reiterated full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guidance of $2.25 to $2.35 and expects free cash flow of more than $18 billion this year, more than $19 billion in 2027, and more than $21 billion in 2028.
